entry.title: Seeing the problem was the easy part

link.title: Seeing the problem was the easy part

entry.content:
Near the end of our busiest run, a tiger walks past a camera. The motion detector next to it sees something move and forwards the frame to the object recognizer. The recognizer will find the tiger. It just won’t get to that frame for another 25 minutes.

The recognizer is working the whole time. It’s answering frames that arrived long before the tiger, and every new frame joins the back of the line.

In my last post, I described a tracker that fell behind while its health checks stayed green, and promised to write about what we learned working on these problems at IMT Atlantique. This is the first half: getting the application to say what’s wrong. The second half, getting the system to do the right thing about it, is still in progress.

A tiger, not an earthquake

Our use case was less dramatic than an earthquake. It was a video surveillance system that watches for dangerous animals and alerts residents and authorities when one shows up.

Each camera sends its frames to its own motion detector at the edge, and the three detectors send the frames where something moved to one object recognizer. In our runs, the recognizer ran in the cloud. It doesn’t have to: it can also run on the edge, next to the detectors. That choice comes back later.

The application is open source. We ran it on Grid’5000 virtual machines with K3s. Camera nodes had 1 CPU and 1 GB of memory, edge nodes 4 CPUs and 8 GB, and cloud nodes 8 CPUs and 16 GB.

What the platform sees, and what matters

Out of the box, Kubernetes tells you about containers: CPU, memory, network, whether the process is up. Those are the numbers an autoscaler acts on. But when a tiger walks past a camera, how long until someone gets the alert? None of them can tell you.

Only the application knows that. So the developers instrument it with OpenTelemetry: frame rate, processing time, detection accuracy, how many frames each motion detector forwards. Those go to Prometheus, next to the infrastructure metrics.

The developer also writes one configuration file for the feedback loop. It says what the objectives are, for example a maximum processing time, and which metrics measure them. It says which services depend on which. And it lists what can be done when something goes wrong: lower the frame rate, switch to a lighter model, or scale a service.

The loop reads the metrics and checks the objectives. When one is missed, it tries to work out which component is responsible and picks an action from that list. To test it, Chaos Mesh injects faults like network latency and CPU pressure.

What the metrics showed

The most useful experiment was also the simplest. We generated footage where animals appear at a controlled rate, a number of expected appearances per hour for each camera, and watched the object recognizer.

With all three cameras at 30 appearances per hour, the recognizer’s response time climbs for the whole run. It ends at about 25 minutes and never comes back down. In the paper’s plots it rises in steps, each time the motion detectors forward a new batch of frames. Even at 5 appearances per hour, it climbed to about 12 minutes before the backlog drained.

That’s the first part of the last post’s story, measured: a service that is working, and falling further behind. Frames with motion arrive faster than the recognizer can answer them, and each new one waits behind all the others. Every cat that crosses a camera is motion too, and it waits in the same line as the tiger. These runs measured the backlog. They didn’t test what to do about it.

So what should the system do?

Seeing the backlog is one thing. Choosing the fix is another, and the right one depends on where the recognizer can run.

The animation below plays out how the loop could respond as conditions change. It’s an illustration of the options, not something we measured.

If the site is connected, the obvious fix is the cloud. Send the frames there and add recognizer replicas until they keep up. The cloud has machines to spare, so this is the case where scaling works. It costs bandwidth and money, and every frame pays the trip over the network.

Sometimes the link is up but slow. Then more replicas don’t help, and neither does a lighter model: the frames spend their time on the network, not in the recognizer. What helps is sending less over the link, which means fewer frames.

Now take the earthquake from the last post. The link to the cloud is damaged or gone, and the recognizer has to run on the edge, next to the detectors. There’s no spare machine to add a replica to, and, as in the last post’s thought experiment, a second copy on the same device can make things worse. What’s left is to do less work per frame, look at fewer frames, or both. A lighter model answers faster, but it gets more wrong: it may take a cat for a tiger and wake people for nothing, or take the tiger for a cat and say nothing. A lower frame rate sends fewer frames to the recognizer, but a tiger that walks past between two frames is never seen.

Each of these fixes costs something different: money, bandwidth, accuracy, or frames nobody looks at. Which cost is acceptable isn’t in any metric. It depends on whether the cloud is reachable right now and how fast the link is, and on how much detection the people relying on the alert can afford to lose. The developer knows that. The platform doesn’t.

What we learned

The first lesson is that the metric that explained the problem came from the developer. Response time moved with how many frames the edge forwards, and that depends on how much moves in front of the cameras. No infrastructure metric measures that. Someone who knows the application had to decide it was worth counting.

The second is that the loop should read the application’s needs from a file, not have them built in. Objectives, dependencies and actions all live in that file, and the metrics the loop watches can change while the system runs, without touching code. When the application changes, you change the file, not the loop.

The third is the one I’d put first: seeing was the easy part. The metrics showed the backlog clearly. Deciding what to do about it depends on things the metrics don’t say: where the recognizer can run, whether the cloud is reachable and how fast, which fixes are even possible right now, and what each one costs in missed detections. The configuration file can list the fixes. Choosing between them automatically, at the right moment, is the hard part, and it was left for later work.

That’s also why I’d call these results preliminary, as the paper does. They come from one application on a handful of virtual machines. They show what the loop can observe, not that it keeps the objectives.

What comes next

Remember the questions from the last post? This work answers part of the first one: with the right metrics, you can see the problem. It doesn’t answer the harder half. Which part of the pipeline is to blame, and which part is only showing the symptom? And it raises the others more sharply. When the cloud is there, is scaling the right call? When it isn’t, which fix do you use, and in what order? When do you undo it? And how do you compare a fix that costs money with one that costs missed detections?

Those are the questions I’ve been working on since, and I’ll write about them once the results are out.

The paper is Application-level observability for adaptive Edge to Cloud continuum systems, UCC ‘25, with a preprint on arXiv.

In the meantime, I’m curious about the other side. If you’ve run something like this at the edge, how did you decide what to give up when it couldn’t keep up? I’d really like to hear about it.
entry.summary: What we learned from making an edge-to-cloud video pipeline report its own health, and why seeing a backlog is not the same as knowing how to fix it.

entry.title: The fix that makes edge failures worse

link.title: The fix that makes edge failures worse

entry.content:
When an application starts falling behind, the platform usually does one of two things: it adds another copy of the service, or it restarts it. In a data center, that works most of the time. I want to talk about the cases where it doesn’t.

Imagine the minutes after an earthquake. The link to the cloud is damaged, and people are leaving buildings that may not hold. Cameras across the district stream video to the one edge device still running nearby. On it, a tracking service detects people, follows them from one camera to the next and works out which way they went, so rescuers know where to look for the ones who didn’t make it out.

Suddenly every camera in the area matters. The tracker can’t keep up, and frames start to pile up. Its health checks are still green.

The autoscaler sees CPU climbing and adds a second copy of the tracker. There’s nowhere else to put it, so it goes on the same device and eats CPU and memory the first copy needed. The cameras now get split between the two copies. Each one keeps its own memory of who it is following, so each sees only part of the path, and neither can say which way people went.

Then the device runs out of memory. The tracker gets killed and restarted, and since everything it knew lived inside the process, it comes back with no idea who it was following or where they were last seen.

Nothing had crashed at the start. The tracker was working, just too slowly, and every automatic fix made things worse.

To be clear, this is a thought experiment, not something I measured. It assumes a simple tracker that keeps its state in memory and a single edge device. A tracker built to share or save its state would lose less. But both assumptions are common at the edge, and the platform has no way of knowing which kind of service it’s dealing with.

The same story works after a flood or a wildfire, or during an attack on a public place. Any time software has to follow people through a camera network while everything around it falls apart.

Why this is hard at the edge

In an emergency, these applications run close to where the data is produced: pipelines that turn camera and sensor streams into something useful, and decision apps that raise an alert, send a team or warn people within seconds. Earthquake early warning has to reach people within seconds. After a disaster, a few seconds can decide whether rescuers find someone in time.

And they run under the worst conditions you could design. The devices are small, sometimes on battery. The network is saturated, unstable, or partly destroyed. Every sensor in the area becomes important at the same moment, and there is nobody on site to open a dashboard and figure out what went wrong.

That’s where the usual self-healing runs out. Kubernetes restarts crashed containers by default, and its autoscaler adds copies once you configure it. But scaling needs spare capacity, and at the edge there may be none. A restart throws away whatever the service had in memory. And many edge failures aren’t crashes at all: the process is healthy, but the link is saturated, the model is too slow for the hardware, or input arrives faster than the pipeline can handle.

There’s also a problem people tend to forget: you can’t start a container without its image. Pulling the image is already the slowest part of starting a container in normal conditions. One study put it at 76% of startup time. Images that bundle an AI model are big. If the image isn’t already cached somewhere near the event, the device has to fetch it over the same broken link, and that can take minutes nobody has.

Scaling isn’t always the wrong answer, though. When a service simply stops, starting a fresh copy is fast and works well. The hard part is telling which kind of failure you’re looking at.

What others have done

None of this is new, and a lot of people have worked on parts of it.

On the orchestrator side, KEDA lets Kubernetes scale on queue length or event rates instead of CPU, which is a better signal, although the only action is still adding or removing copies. KubeEdge keeps edge nodes and their apps running when the link to the cloud drops. For images, Dragonfly lets nodes share image layers peer to peer, and research on the edge has gone further with collaborative lazy pulling, which starts a container before the whole image has arrived, and adaptive image placement across the cloud-edge continuum. All of these still assume the image, or part of it, is somewhere nearby.

Several teams have built self-adaptive loops around Kubernetes, for example to decide between scaling and offloading AI tasks across edge devices. CODECO and QONNECT take application-level quality of service into account when placing workloads. Most of this work still acts on the infrastructure, meaning where things run and with how many resources. The closest thing I’ve found to what I care about is BumbleBee from Microsoft Research, which lets developers attach their own adaptation logic to a container so the orchestrator can use it.

On the application side, many systems adapt themselves. Spatula tracks people across cameras by only processing the cameras where they’re likely to show up next. Distream shifts video analytics work between cameras and the edge as load changes. Chameleon and AWStream lower resolution or frame rate to fit the resources available. The catch is that this logic lives inside each application, and the orchestrator doesn’t know it exists.

Connecting the two is where a lot of current research is. Rainbow did it early on at the architecture level. More recently there’s been a wave of work on cloud microservices that goes from diagnosis to action automatically, often with LLM agents, and benchmarks like MicroRemed that measure how well it works. I’ve seen much less of it at the edge, where a pipeline spans several tiers, resources are tight and nobody is around to decide.

The questions I’m left with

The first is diagnosis. When the whole pipeline slows down, how does the system figure out which part is actually to blame, and not just which part shows the symptom? And can it do that without training data, when no two emergencies look alike?

Then what to do about it. If restarting and scaling are off the table, what else is there? Developers usually know better fixes: compress the video, lower the resolution, switch to a lighter model, skip an optional step. I still don’t think we have a good way to hand that knowledge to an automatic system. Should an application be allowed to degrade itself on purpose to keep delivering results? If so, who decides what’s acceptable to lose?

When several fixes are possible, which one goes first? Fixed rules written by a person, or a system that learns from past incidents? And once a fix has worked, when do you undo it?

There’s deployment too. What should be decided in advance and what should be left to runtime? Which images should already be sitting near places where a disaster could happen, and with the little storage edge devices have, which ones do you leave out?

Last, evaluation. Scaling is sometimes the right call, so how do you make sure a system still picks it when it should? And how do you build a fair test between infrastructure fixes and application-level fixes, one that doesn’t quietly favor the approach you’re hoping will win?

Where this comes from

I worked on these questions as an R&D engineer at IMT Atlantique, on feedback mechanisms for edge-to-cloud applications. We built video-processing pipelines across edge and cloud, instrumented them, and pushed them until they broke on Grid’5000. Part of that work is in our UCC ‘25 paper, Application-level observability for adaptive Edge to Cloud continuum systems (there’s also a preprint on arXiv).

I’ll write about what we learned in another post. If you’ve run critical services at the edge and had to keep them alive without being able to restart or scale, I’d really like to hear how you did it.
entry.summary: When restarting or scaling is not an option, how do you deploy critical data-processing and decision-making apps at the edge and keep them from failing?

entry.title: Started a New Position at Inria

link.title: Started a New Position at Inria

entry.content:
I’m excited to share that I started a new position as a Research and Development Engineer at Inria on December 1st, 2024.

In this role, I’ll be contributing to the CoAnsible project — an effort to bridge the gap between configuration tools and adaptive computing in cloud-edge continuum environments.

Stay tuned for more updates as I dive into this new chapter!

📍 Where: Inria, France
📅 Start Date: December 1, 2024
🔬 Role: Research & Development Engineer

Feel free to connect with me if you’re working on something similar or curious about the project.

entry.title: Feedback Mechanisms for Edge-to-Cloud Applications at IMT Atlantique

link.title: Feedback Mechanisms for Edge-to-Cloud Applications at IMT Atlantique

entry.content:
On December 1st, 2023, I joined IMT Atlantique as a Research and Development Engineer to work on feedback mechanisms for Edge-to-Cloud video processing applications.

The project focused on improving the monitoring, analysis, and adaptation of distributed applications across heterogeneous environments. I had the opportunity to design and implement a full feedback loop that connects metrics collection, performance monitoring, and automated reactions.

🔍 Project Objectives

  • Improve observability of distributed video pipelines (motion detection, object recognition)
  • Enable dynamic feedback to ensure performance and quality objectives are met
  • Detect and respond to SLO violations through actionable insights

⚙️ My Contributions

  • Designed a monitoring pipeline using Prometheus and OpenTelemetry
  • Implemented metrics collection on FPS, latency, processing time, and object recognition quality
  • Developed a Flask-based interface for visualizing critical metrics and system health
  • Created a prototype integrating:
    • A camera simulator
    • Motion detection at the edge
    • Cloud-based object recognition (YOLOv5)
  • Traced processing flow end-to-end using distributed tracing

🛠️ Tools & Technologies

  • Python, Flask
  • Prometheus & OpenTelemetry
  • Docker, Docker Compose
  • GitLab CI/CD
  • YOLOv5, OpenCV
  • Grafana (for metric dashboards)

📘 Outcomes

  • Developed and documented an open-source prototype:
    GitLab Repository
  • Explored potential extensions using critical metric detection and SLI/SLO reasoning
  • Shared findings internally and supported future directions at IMT Atlantique and Inria

This experience helped shape my current work on resilient, adaptive applications, and provided a solid foundation for my ongoing research on intelligent configuration and monitoring systems.

Feel free to reach out if you’re working on similar topics!
entry.summary: My research and engineering work at IMT Atlantique on monitoring and adaptation for distributed video processing systems
